Immigrant advocacy groups have alleged that unaccompanied children and their sponsors are among those being targeted under the administration's aggressive immigration crackdown.
In June, DHS agents visited the offices of several Washington-area nonprofit organizations that provide legal services to unaccompanied migrant children.
Last year, ABC News reported that the administration was directing immigration agents to track down unaccompanied migrant children in the United States.

"We are seeing children being bullied in court to take self-deportation and other children showing up without any counsel, even though the government is mandated to provide them with an attorney," Lukens said. "Unaccompanied immigrant children need meaningful and expert advocacy through the court system, not political games."

title: Trump to announce new $15B steel plant: White House official
summary: The project, which will be built by Mesabi Metallics in Iowa, is the first mega-steel plant built in the United States since the 1960s.
story: The project will be built by Mesabi Metallics in Iowa.
President Donald Trump will announce the construction of a massive new steel plant during an Oval Office event on Monday, a White House official said.

The project, which will be built by Mesabi Metallics in Iowa, will command a $15 billion investment from the company and is the first mega-steel plant built in the United States since the 1960s, the official said. The first steel production is expected to be in 2030 and, once fully built out, will produce 10 million tons of steel annually, making it among the largest in the U.S.

The company also recently invested $2.5 billion in a new iron ore mine in Minnesota, which the official said will allow the project to be fully integrated in the U.S. from mining to production. The mine is expected to produce 7.5 million tons of iron ore annually and will create 350 new jobs in Minnesota. Another 1,750 jobs are expected in Iowa, the official added.

"Today’s announcement underscores the President's historic efforts to revitalize the U.S. steel industry -- supporting local communities, strengthening supply chains, and protecting our national security," White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a statement confirming the announcement.

Executives from Mesabi Metallics are expected to attend the event on Monday, as well as Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Executive Director of the White House's National Energy Dominance Council Jarrod Agen and John Jovanovic, chairman of the U.S. Export-Import Bank.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the details of the project.

The Wall Street Journal noted that Mesabi Metallics is backed by the Essar Group, an Indian multinational conglomerate, which first proposed the mine and mill project 20 years ago, and ultimately failed. The mine project filed for bankruptcy a decade ago, the Wall Street Journal reported.

title: Sen. Mark Kelly says Democrats have to 'do a better job'
summary: On "This Week," Sen. Mark Kelly discussed the midterms, war with Iran and AI.
story: “I think there's going to be a big turnout" for midterms, Kelly said.
Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz, said Sunday that the Democratic party needs to do a “better job” if they were to win control of Congress in November’s midterm elections.

“I think we have to have answers. We have to have, we have to pass legislation. We have to send it to the president's desk. Hopefully, if it benefits the American people, he will sign it,” Kelly told “This Week” co-anchor Martha Raddatz.

Many of November’s elections are shaping up to be tight races, with some recent polls indicating Democrats could come out on top. Charlie Cook, founder of the Cook Political Report, also appeared on “This Week” Sunday and predicted that Democrats would win both the House of Representatives and the Senate -- something he said earlier this week would be less a as “blue wave,” but rather a “red undertow.”
“It's hitting some places more than other places, but it isn't pro-Democrat. It's anti-Trump basically, and Republicans that have been supported by the president,” Cook said.
Kelly said that many Americans are frustrated with the Republican party and administration.

“I think there's going to be a big turnout. I think some of these races are going to be close, and it really comes down to the fact that the American people are just struggling and Republicans and this president don't have an answer,” Kelly said.
Kelly also cited the war with Iran as a big factor that could be driving voters to pull the lever for Democrats.

“War and tariffs caused by Donald Trump and enabled by the Republicans in the United States Congress are just killing the American people. I mean, they cannot afford their lives, and when you can't, when you're having a hard time feeding your kid, I mean, nothing else really matters,” Kelly said.

The war with Iran has severely limited the flow of oil through the critical Strait of Hormuz, spiking oil prices. This week at the United Nations, Iran’s president proposed a seven-day plan to reopen the strait, which President Trump rejected.
“Well, I'm rejecting their deal. They want to make a deal where we open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly,” said Trump on Saturday.
“The president got into this without a strategic goal, without a plan, without a timeline, without an exit strategy. He's stuck,” said Kelly.
“This thing has been a disaster and it's been a mistake, and it's because of the failed leadership of this president,” Kelly added.

Prior to the war with Iran, "the straits were open and we didn't have" dead and wounded service members, Kelly further said. "This thing has been a disaster, and it's been a mistake, and it's because of the failed leadership of this president.”

Raddatz also asked Kelly about artificial intelligence and Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. In a lavish state visit last week, Xi met with the president in Washington, D.C., with many hoping progress would be made on a deal to regulate the development of AI. Kelly said that he thinks the two leaders instead agreed to set up “sort of a working group.”

“That's not an agreement. It doesn't look like they had a serious discussion about this. This technology is moving very, very quickly. It could be very disruptive to hardworking Americans, could lose their jobs,” said Kelly. “There's safety concerns about this, and the White House, specifically the president, doesn't seem to think we should put any guardrails in place."

Kelly also expressed the desire to stay ahead of China in AI development -- a sentiment echoed by Trump. In a post on social media, the president claimed in part "there is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so."
"At the same time, we can't allow the Chinese to win the race to getting the best AI technology. That would be a mistake," Kelly added.

title: Blanche addresses White House press ban, calls access 'a privilege ... not a right'
summary: Attorney General Todd Blanched joined "This Week" Sunday amid ongoing litigation between several media outlets and the administration over access to the White House.
story: The attorney general disputed that the president "denied access" to outlets.

Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday addressed the Trump administration's decision to ban three mainstream news outlets from accessing the White House, saying that President Donald Trump had not "denied access" to the organizations and asserting that it is a "privilege ... not a right" to be at the White House.

"The president hasn't denied access. That's not the right way to describe it. This is -- what the president has said is that he is sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news," Blanche said in an exclusive interview with "This Week" co-anchor Martha Raddatz. "There's still obviously litigation going on, but the important thing, Martha, is to know that ... being in the White House is a privilege. It's not a right."

In the early hours Thursday, Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order that required the White House to temporarily restore credentials of journalists working for CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Kelly said in his ruling that he believed the outlets cleared the "high bar" required to grant a TRO.

Journalists were allowed back onto the White House grounds later Thursday and primary television pool coverage resumed Friday for the final day of Chinese President Xi Jinping's official state visit. But on Saturday, there was no TV pool coverage for the president's trip to a football game in Tennessee; CNN was scheduled to be network covering the president that day, but they said their access to Air Force One was blocked.
Blanche said it wasn't unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed onto the president's plane.

"The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One. This wasn't a a one-time denial of CNN. There's all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying," according to Blanche, who added, "it's not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it's common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president."
Blanche claimed the three news outlets that were subject to the White House ban "refuse to report anything accurately," which he said presented a "national security problem."

"When you have complete misinformation coming out of the White House that affects our relationship with our foreign partners, that affects our relationship with our foreign enemies -- and so this is just not about the fact that they're refusing to report accurate news. It's all about the information that the American people have a right to hear coming out of of our what should be respected media outlets."
Judge Kelly, however, was skeptical in his TRO ruling that national security was the true reason for the ban.

"For one thing, nothing in the record that predates this suit suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns. Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was 'banning' Plaintiffs from the White House -- instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs’ reporting," Kelly wrote.
Hours after announcing the ban on social media, Trump was asked in the Oval Office if there was any "particular reason or particular story" that prompted it.
"No, no. It's -- it's really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it," the president said.

On "This Week," Blanche said he wouldn't "get into what the judge says" because the litigation is ongoing, but added "our position has been clear from the beginning. What they say is exactly the issue when it comes to national security."
When Raddatz pressed Blanche to provide specific examples of stories with which the White House has taken issue, Blanche declined to do so.

On the issue of artificial intelligence, the attorney general echoed the president's position on the technology, describing it as "so important and vital to our national security interests and to the success of this country that the United States lead in this space."
Trump has said it's critical that the U.S. continues to dominate the AI space, citing competition with China specifically.

"Whoever wins AI, WINS! We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I’m going to keep it that way! I’m not going to stifle Growth, of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution, or the Internet, itself," he posted on social media Monday.

Some AI company leaders are calling for an industry-wide slowdown amid growing concerns about how the rapid pace of development. Multiple incidents of AI agents acting autonomously have come to light in recent months, including instances where AI agents infiltrated outside companies without the agents' parent companies' awareness as it happened.

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that OpenAI agent "infiltrated" a government public health website earlier this summer. This weekend, OpenAI confirmed that its models interacted with U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, behavior the company discovered amid an ongoing review into its AI agents' behaviors.

Blanche acknowledged that "there's going to be adjustments that have to be made" around AI as the industry continues to develop, but he argued the companies themselves already have the ability to "adjust the technology" as needed.

"In the meantime, the answer is not to just try to all of a sudden try to regulate this in a way that will make us second or third place in the world as far as being being the leaders in this space," Blanche said.
During his speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York Tuesday, Trump said of AI, "We're going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice."

Asked what that meant, Blanche said, "What it means is that we have a ton of laws -- criminal laws, civil laws -- that are already in place and on the books that allow us to charge individuals, to charge companies in the right circumstances when there's crimes committed, and so the answer isn't always more laws, more laws, more laws."

"When there are crimes committed, we have a lot of tools already, and the federal Title 18 gives us a lot of a lot of ways to go after criminals and bad actors in the AI space and other spaces," Blanche continued. "So when the president talks about about the fact that the Department of Justice and the FBI and [Homeland Security Investigations], they can go and arrest bad actors in this space, that's what he means, and it's true, and that's what we're doing."

title: White House orders over $800M in funds rescinded
summary: The White House announced Friday evening that it was rescinding over $800 million in congressionally appropriated funds across a range of government programs.
story: The move has already drawn criticism from at least one GOP senator.
The White House announced Friday evening that it was rescinding over $800 million in congressionally appropriated funds across a range of government programs.

In a statement, the White House said President Donald Trump was invoking authority under the Impoundment Control Act to deploy a "pocket rescission" of funds, a legally questionable maneuver Trump also used in 2025 to claw back billions in appropriated funds for foreign aid programs.

The Supreme Court effectively allowed that rescission to proceed -- staying a lower court order last September requiring those funds to be obligated -- but noted that the "order should not be read as a final determination on the merits" of the rescission.

Pocket rescissions occur when the president requests Congress to cancel funds as the end of the fiscal year approaches, according to the Government Accountability Office. While Congress needs to approve rescissions, it only has 45 days to respond, and "when not enough time is given to consider this request or for funds to be used before they expire, the president is bypassing congressional authority over government funding," the GAO notes.

According to the release from the White House, the new rescissions target programs across a variety of federal agencies, including the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Education, the Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Department of Justice.

Among them are $567 million in funds to HHS which the administration alleges went to "pro-illegal immigration programs and Non-Governmental Organizations that provided services to refugees, asylees, and other non-citizens and put unaccompanied children in harm's way."
The administration also lists programs under the DHS which it claimed "laundered taxpayer dollars" to provide "welfare" to undocumented immigrants.

Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins -- who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee -- blasted the move in a statement on social media on Friday, calling it an attempt to "undermine Congress's Constitutional power of the purse" and a violation of the law.

"The independent Government Accountability Office has concluded that pocket rescissions are unlawful and not permitted by the Impoundment Control Act," Collins wrote. "Any effort to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law."

Collins said that Congress received the $810 million package of rescissions from the White House's Office of Management and Budget with no warning and alleged that "OMB intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law."
"OMB is an agency of the executive branch.  It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding," she said, adding that she will "work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions."

title: Candidates are increasingly dropping debates. Here's what it means for voters
summary: Fewer than half of Senate races will have candidate debates this year.
story: Fewer than half of Senate races will have candidate debates this year.

As the high-stakes midterm elections approach and hundreds of candidates make their case to voters, in many cases, those voters won't get a chance to see candidates debate -- a trend over the last several elections, according to an ABC News analysis.

This year, 36 governors are up for election -- 21 of those races will not see a debate between the two major-party candidates. That number includes three of the governor's races ranked by ABC News as toss-ups: Georgia, Nevada and Ohio.

The number of governor’s races with no debate has increased over the past two midterm elections. In 2018, only two races out of 36 saw no debates -- Alabama and Nevada. In 2022, that number went up to eight out of the 36 gubernatorial races.
The trend is even more pronounced in Senate races.
Of the 35 Senate seats up for election in 2026, 21 of them have no debate scheduled between the major candidates including toss-up races in Ohio and Texas.
Of the 34 seats up for reelection in 2024, nine had no debates; in 2022, there were no debates for 14 out of 35.

While candidates skipping debates may help spare them from gaffes or missteps, it can be to the detriment of voters -- who, an expert told ABC News, are missing an opportunity to not only learn about candidates' platforms, but also how they handle pressure.
The candidates who have declined debates ahead of the midterms in November have cited a variety of reasons.

In Ohio, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton declined to debate her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy, saying she did not want to "platform" his "baseless lies" -- a reference to what she called false claims in some of his political ads. Ramaswamy has challenged Acton to debate him.

Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who is running for governor in Alabama, opted against debating Democratic opponent Doug Jones, telling a local TV station that "there's so much difference between us. I mean, there's no reason to get up there and argue about differences of opinion." Jones has continued to call for debates.

In Texas' closely watched Senate race, Republican candidate Ken Paxton had initially committed to a debate against state Sen. James Talarico earlier this summer. Despite Paxton's commitment, ABC affiliate WFAA says their offers to host a debate have gone unanswered by Paxton's team.
On Thursday, Talarico challenged Paxton to a debate on Fox News. Paxton’s campaign has not responded to requests for comment on his plans to debate.
Paxton did not participate in debates in his previous runs for office as attorney general.

In Arizona, Gov. Katie Hobbs is declining a debate in her race -- marking the second election cycle she has done so. In her 2022 race, she requested separate televised interviews of herself and her opponent, Kari Lake. When Lake declined, Hobbs opted not to debate.

This year, Hobbs again declined to debate, her campaign manager saying it was because "face-to-face engagement with Arizonans is more effective than a stage designed for short soundbites and political theater."
But no matter the reason for candidates' decisions not to debate, the result is the same: voters are denied the opportunity to see a head-to-head comparison of the top contenders on their ballot.

Craig Hennigan, a lecturer in communications at the University of Nevada Las Vegas and director of their award-winning debate team, said when candidates skip debates, voters don't get to see how they "react under pressure."

"[Voters are] not actually looking to watch a debate to learn about issues. However, the research has shown that people do incidentally learn about issues -- but they're more interested in the character being presented," Hennigan told ABC News.
The same setting that creates moments of genuine insight for voters can put candidates in an unpredictable and vulnerable position, Hennigan said.

"[Candidates are] not certain what their opponent's going to say, and whatever message they've been trying to curate, when they're put on the spot, they might have a misstep. So there's risk involved with having to perform in a debate,” he said.

Hennigan argues that the incentives look different for candidates heading into debates depending on their position, saying "if you have a very substantial lead, there is very little that you can gain as a candidate from participating in a debate" citing President Donald Trump declining to participate in primary debates in 2024 as an example.
His advice for candidates who do opt for a debate? "You don't attempt to win. You just attempt to not lose. You are trying to avoid gaffes."

title: House Dems plan oversight of Trump administration; impeachment an option
summary: Democrats are preparing an agenda if the party sweeps control in November.
story: Democrats are preparing an agenda if the party sweeps control in November.

WASHINGTON -- House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda, with investigations of President Donald Trump, his family and his administration if the party sweeps control of the chamber from Republicans in the November elections.

The undertaking is as robust as it is daunting, spanning several House committees. With majority power comes bigger budgets and staff, and the ability to investigate, subpoena and potentially course-correct what the Democrats say are widespread corruption and abuses of power. Impeachment of the Republican president and Cabinet officials is not off the table.

“There is a cost to the American people of the out-of-control corruption,” said Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker if Democrats win control at the Capitol.
“If folks have been stealing from the American people, shortchanging the American people or screwing over the American people,” Jeffries said, “we are going to hold the crooks accountable.”

Congress has enormous ability to conduct oversight of the executive branch as part of its power as a coequal branch of government, and a road map for the Democratic-run investigations has already been set by the almost daily letters lawmakers send to the administration and in amicus court filings.

Democrats are asking about the money-making by Trump and his family, whose wealth has grown dramatically since he returned to the White House in January 2025. They are investigating the potential civil rights violations of Americans killed protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and of detained immigrants being deported to faraway countries. They have fought the closing of the Kennedy Center, launched investigations into private funding of the America at 250 celebrations and tracked the shuttering of federal operations, including the U.S. Agency for International Development.

New questions emerge daily, including the Trump family’s recent acknowledgment that a weekend wedding party for the president’s son Donald Trump Jr. was partly funded by a Russian oligarch, with reportedly close ties to the Kremlin.
Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is in line to become the chairman of the Judiciary Committee, characterized the issues involved as “gargantuan."
“We need to zero in quickly on the forms of systemic corruption that have cost the public huge amounts of money," Raskin told The Associated Press, “and where there are legislative cures available.”

Jeffries will almost certainly be under pressure from the far left to move more swiftly to articles of impeachment against Trump, who during his first term became the first president to be twice impeached by the House. Both times, he was acquitted by the Senate.

Impeaching the president a third time may not hold the currency that it once did. Democrats will more likely focus their impeachment efforts on Cabinet members. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth already faces articles of impeachment from a Republican, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, over his leadership at the Pentagon and his management of the Iran war.
“We haven’t ruled anything out,” Jeffries said recently about the tools available to Congress, “and we haven’t ruled anything in.”

The White House is likely to play hardball if confronted with investigations, and Democrats are bracing for an administration that potentially ignores subpoenas or refuses to turn over paperwork that lawmakers are demanding.
The Democrats are also reaching beyond the administration into various corporate and business entities for potential wrongdoing.
Ranking Democratic lawmakers who are in line to lead committees if power shifts are beginning to chart the investigations they plan to tackle.

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat now on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has outlined five priorities, including Trump family business dealings, the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and ICE operations.
“We’re already doing work,” Garcia told the AP.
He also mentioned the Department of Health and Human Services under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as well as broader allegations of corporate corruption.

The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, whose jurisdiction includes the State Department, said the committee plans to investigate Trump's international dealings, including around the Iran war.

He expects the committee will also look into the administration's Venezuela operations — from the military strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific waters to the U.S. partnership with a private company to develop and access the South American country's oil.

Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking Democrat at the Natural Resources Committee, which oversees the Interior Department and its National Park Service operations, has begun digging into Trump's “vanity projects,” including the demolition of the White House's East wing for a new ballroom and the president's proposed arch.
Huffman and other committee members have also been eyeing the Trump family's role in various minerals deals.

At the committee's last session before lawmakers recessed to campaign for the midterm elections, Huffman said that if Democrats take charge, he plans to call witnesses, put them under oath and follow the evidence where it leads.
"When people ask what will we do," he said he responds, “My answer is simple. We’ll use those tools. We’ll act like the Congress.”

title: Supreme Court allows use of citizenship database ahead of midterms
summary: The Supreme Court has given the Trump administration a green light to use a federal citizenship database to verify voters ahead of the midterm elections.
story: The ruling will nonetheless likely have a "minimal" impact," one justice said.
The Supreme Court has given the Trump administration a green light to use a federal citizenship database to verify voters ahead of the midterm elections.

In a 6-3 opinion, the Supreme Court lifted a lower court order that blocked the Department of Homeland Security from expanding a 40-year-old immigration database -- known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system -- to help states screen voter records for noncitizens.

"The District Court's order thus inhibits the Federal Government's efforts to assist state and local agencies in the proper administration of the midterm elections. Under these circumstances, the equities weigh in favor of a stay," the majority wrote.

While the ruling gives the Department of Homeland Security authority to use the database ahead of the midterms, the court's conservative majority noted that the impact of the ruling was blunted by another federal law -- the National Voter Registration Act -- which prohibits states from purging voters within 90 days of the election.
President Donald Trump has characterized noncitizen voting as a pressing threat to free and fair elections, but audits of voter rolls have suggested that voting by noncitizens is exceedingly rare.
The court, ruling along ideological lines, rejected an argument that federal law prohibited the Trump administration from a revamping citizenship database to verify voters.

In an unsigned opinion, the majority wrote that Congress, in the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act, authorized the "an information-sharing regime like the modified SAVE program."

The majority also concluded that the Trump administration would suffer irreparable harm if they were barred from using the database because the lower court ruling "inhibits the Federal Government's efforts to assist state and local agencies in the proper administration of the midterm elections."

Due to the National Voter Registration Act's prohibition against purging voter roles this close to an election, the ruling only allows the Trump administration to conduct "individualized inquiries" to verify voters, rather than perform the bulk searches the system was created to conduct. As a result, according to the court's liberal wing, the ruling "will likely have a minimal, short-term impact."

Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson, Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan dissented from the majority, rejecting the argument that Congress allowed such a database. They wrote that the majority misreads the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act to override "the limits that privacy laws impose on the sharing of citizenship information with DHS."
"But there is no reason to believe that Congress meant to repeal laws that would otherwise prohibit federal agencies from disclosing citizenship information," Justice Jackson wrote.
She also pushed back on the notion that the Trump administration, not individual voters, would be irreparably harmed by the decision.

"In my view, however, the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take," she wrote.

title: Trump-Xi takeaways: White House touts progress on AI, Iran and exports
summary: The stakes were high during the meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
story: The meeting initially appeared to have few tangible takeaways.

The stakes were high during the meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, with the White House later claiming progress was made on talks related to artificial intelligence and global concerns, including the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran, despite initially remaining silent on any tangible victories.
It's remains uncertain what went on behind closed doors, but many Republicans had clear expectations that Trump would put pressure on Xi.
Those expectations may have been tempered by the lavish welcome the Chinese dictator received from Trump for Xi's first visit to the United States in more than a decade.

The president traveled to Joint Base Andrews to greet Xi and his wife in person as American service members literally rolled out the red carpet minutes before the Chinese leader stepped off the plane. A military choir serenaded Xi and a who's who guest list of American business leaders, billionaires and Washington elite at a glitzy state dinner in the East Room of the White House.
Trump took Xi on a tour of his construction projects, including his White House ballroom and helipad, exclaiming Xi "loves good granite."
Indeed, Xi seemed impressed.

"I want to thank the honorable president and the first lady for everything they've done for myself and my wife during this visit. Everything is down to the highest order of perfection," Xi said through a translator at the White House on Friday. "And there is thought in every little detail. And it's greatly appreciated."

Trump's take at the end of the visit was, "We've had a tremendous visit from two spectacular people, and we've really enjoyed it. And I think we've made tremendous strides. We've made great strides, very positive for both countries."
Trump did not elaborate. He echoed those sentiments on his social media platform and added only that he and Xi plan to meet in person twice more before the end of the year.

When asked by a reporter if the two leaders discussed the war in Iran, Trump said, "We did, we did," and adding "I think we're going to do great," when pressed on potential progress in the Strait of Hormuz.

David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, said in an interview on Fox News on Friday the U.S. has evidence China "directly or indirectly" has supported Iran in the war, and that Trump challenged Xi on the issue during this summit.
"President Trump made it clear it is unacceptable to us to have any interaction with Iran with support of the war," Perdue said. He insisted China made a "commitment not to engage in assistance."

At one point, Trump told reporters the U.S. and China will continue "speaking a lot" before suggesting potential action between the two countries in the agriculture industry without offering any specifics.
"We'll be speaking a lot. I think our farmers are going to be very happy. A lot of very positive things happened," he said.

On the topic of artificial intelligence, Trump was less focused on making public assurances that the two technology leaders could fend off warnings about the end of humanity from tech leaders, and more interested in getting Xi to go along with his plan to rebrand the industry as "super intelligence."

In another social media post, Trump said Xi "seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE. That would be "SUPER!," Trump wrote.
Chinese state media reported Xi told Trump that AI must be kept under human control.
According to Xinhau, Xi told Trump that a people-centered approach should be upheld, and AI should be developed for the positive and for good, so that AI will serve the progress of humanity.
Some Republicans had hoped that Trump would exert pressure on Xi on some of these matters.

"China is an adversary, and we have to be very clear-eyed about that. And we have to press them on issues whether its military, whether its trade, whether its AI or anything else we have to be very clear-eyed and we have to press them hard," Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., said Thursday.
Florida Republican Sen. Rick Scott said he understands that Trump has to be diplomatic, "but Xi's a despicable person that is killing us with fentanyl and building a military to try to defeat us."
Overnight, the White House published a fact sheet on its website, marking what it says were some of the accomplishments from the meeting.
It included commitments from China to purchase 10 million metric tons of American coal in 2026 and 2027 and noted progress on China's export controls on fentanyl precursor chemicals.
The readout also said "the two leaders discussed on-going global concerns, including Russia, North Korea, and Iran."
And, according to the fact sheet, the two countries "also agreed to establish a bilateral communication channel" for issues related to artificial intelligence.
The fact sheet also lauded the expected arrival of two giant pandas, leased by China to the Atlanta Zoo.
Editor's Note: This story has been updated with the White House's fact sheet detailing what it says were accomplishments from the meeting.

title: People with Down syndrome and other disabilities find rhythm in Indiana dance program
summary: There's a program in Indiana for people with physical or intellectual disabilities to learn how to dance
story: There's a program in Indiana for people with physical or intellectual disabilities to learn how to dance
FISHERS, Ind. -- Finn Vester, who has autism and Down syndrome, tried a martial arts class but it proved unsuitable because he learns differently, his mother said.
Then he joined Dance Abilities, a program at Academy of Dance Arts in the Indianapolis suburb of Fishers for people with physical or intellectual disabilities.
Now dance has become his way to communicate and connect with others, his mom, Nicole Vester, said.

Claire Graham, the founder of Dance Abilities, got the idea for the program in high school after realizing while she was studying dance, she was never able to connect with her sister with Down syndrome while she took part in her own activities. The program has grown in three years from a summer camp for eight youngsters to year-round classes for about 20 people.

Dance Abilities has separate classes for children ages 18 months to 4, ages 4-7 and 8-12, teenagers, and for adults, too. A successful day for Graham, who has a degree in dance and a master's in recreational therapy, is when everyone has had fun and been challenged.
“I’m not looking for perfection of position and not looking for a perfect performance,” Graham said. “Only a performance that they can feel confident about.”

These dancers are not the only ones performing through challenges. Ezra Frech, a two-time gold medal Paralympian, is competing on this season's “Dancing with the Stars” on ABC. Frech, a track and field athlete, has a prosthetic leg.
Finn's mom values her son’s confidence-building that will help him be able to go into the world and learn new things, she said.

“Claire teaches him at his level. She teaches him a little slower. She teaches him a couple more extra times. And he feels proud and he feels accomplished and he feels like he’s part of a group,” Vester said.
Accommodations at Dance Abilities include slowing down, using more visual cues than verbal instruction, and teacher “helpers” who physically guide students through the movements.
“Sometimes, we’ll add something new that they can work on to make it a little harder,” said one helper, Catherine Benko, 16.
Dance is good for the body, too, with different needs for different students.
For students with Down syndrome, who tend to be naturally more flexible and less strong, Graham emphasizes developing muscle tone. Students with autism, she said, often need more help stretching.
Abigail MacGregor, who has Down syndrome, loves to dance through an obstacle course and to perform her latest moves for friends and family after she’s been practicing all week.
“I just love dance,” Abby said. “The best thing of dance is having fun, being with all my dance crew.”
Tucker McGarrell, 13, who has Down syndrome, doesn’t walk but runs into his dance classes, his mom Amanda McGarrell said.
“It’s not speech therapy or physical therapy or occupational therapy appointments. This is actually something he enjoys doing,” McGarrell said.
McGarrell loves to see her son have an accepting, accommodating place.

“It’s just such a huge thing that Tucker’s given a space and a stage to be himself and get to be with friends and learn new things,” McGarrell said. “It just like fills me with joy knowing that he’s getting to do something that he loves too just like typical kids do.”
Whoever her students are, Graham said, “if you give them the chance to succeed and meet them where they are, they can 100% grow.”
Seeing her students smile is the ultimate metric of success.
“It warms my heart to hear my kiddos saying, 'Look, Mom, I did it!'” she said.
Gruver reported from Fort Collins, Colorado.

title: Global benchmarks are mixed despite Wall Street's rally finish last week
summary: Global shares are trading mixed Monday after a cooldown in oil prices last week helped U.S. stock close out their first winning week in the last three
story: Global shares are trading mixed Monday after a cooldown in oil prices last week helped U.S. stock close out their first winning week in the last three
TOKYO -- Global shares were trading mixed Monday after a cooldown in oil prices last week helped U.S. stocks close out their first winning week in the last three.

France's CAC 40 edged up 0.3% in early trading to 8,097.99, while the German DAX added 0.2% to 25,464.53. Britain's FTSE 100 rose 0.3% to 10,725.57. U.S. shares were set to drift lower with Dow futures dipped 0.3% to 51,992.00. S&P 500 futures shed 0.4% to 7,770.75.
Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 declined 0.7% to finish at 65,877.62.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.2% to 8,679.70. South Korea's Kospi dipped 2.7% to 6,889.74. Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose 0.5% to 24,642.51, while the Shanghai Composite lost 1.7% to 3,823.62.
In energy trading, benchmark U.S. crude gained 3.41% to $95.56 a barrel. Brent xrude, the international standard, rose 3.73% to $108.21 a barrel.

Last week, Brent oil had momentarily dropped to $97-levels. The price is volatile because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow oil to flow freely again from the Middle East, including access to the Strait of Hormuz.
In currency trading, the U.S. dollar fell to 156.93 Japanese yen from 157.19 yen. The euro cost $1.1377, down from $1.1393.

Analysts say market players are closely watching upcoming inflation indicators to see if global central banks will stay hawkish, as they have been. Also of interest of late are AI shares, as those companies continue to post strong earnings, despite public expressions from various influential people about the risks of the technology.
