title: Far-left legal 'cartel' in the hot seat as Trump admin decides its law school gatekeeper status
summary: The Trump Education Department now has 90 days to decide whether to strip the American Bar Association of its decades-long law school accreditation monopoly.
story: Fox News Digital spoke to Public Interest Legal Foundation’s J. Christian Adams about his group’s report warning of far-left indoctrination at top election law schools in the United States.

The future of the nation's primary law school accreditor now rests in the hands of the Trump Education Department after a federal panel deadlocked 8-8 on whether to strip the American Bar Association (ABA) of its gatekeeper status following dozens of federal compliance failures.

The deadlock hands the decision to Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent, who has up to 90 days to decide whether to revoke the ABA’s decades-long accreditation monopoly over roughly 200 law schools nationwide. In a statement to Fox News Digital, a Department of Education spokesperson confirmed that staff had already recommended stripping the ABA's gatekeeper status after finding the group out of compliance with "more than 26 recognition criteria."

The advisory body — known formally as the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI) — advises the Education Department on whether higher education accreditors meet federal standards. NACIQI Chairman Jay Greene told Fox News Digital that while the panel split 8-8 on what action to take, committee members across the board shared a core concern over how the ABA is structured.

"The primary issue that troubled all members of NACIQI is that the ABA accrediting body is clearly not separate and independent from the ABA as a whole," Greene said, noting that federal law requires institutional accreditors to operate independently of trade associations. "Everyone on the committee agreed that this was a problem that required changes. The main divide was over whether the ABA was willing and able to take those steps to remedy the problem or not."
WATCH: BRANDON GILL CORNERS LAW SCHOOL GATEKEEPER WITH DEI QUESTION SHE WON'T ANSWER

A federal advisory panel deadlocked on whether to strip the ABA of its accreditation power, leaving its gatekeeper status in the hands of the Trump Education Department. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Responding to panel criticisms of chronic noncompliance, Melissa Hart, chair of the ABA Accreditation Council, defended the organization's historic track record.

"The Council has been continuously recognized by the Department of Education since 1952, being found in compliance during every regular recognition cycle for the past 74 years," Hart said in a statement. "We take accreditation and our recognition as an accreditor very seriously, and we continue to be a reliable authority for accrediting J.D. programs."

However, legal advocacy groups argue the ABA's structural defects and recent policy shifts render it unfit to serve as an industry gatekeeper. Reed Rubinstein, senior vice president of America First Legal and former general counsel at the Department of Education, told Fox News Digital that the ABA has "disqualified itself and undermined public faith and trust in the legal profession."
EXPLOSIVE REPORT EXPOSES ‘DANGEROUS IMBALANCE’ IN LAW SCHOOL PIPELINE SHAPING HOW ELECTION CASES ARE DECIDED

Rubinstein also dismissed the ABA's recent move to repeal its controversial diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) accreditation standard as a "ruse to retain power," arguing it does not cure the underlying legal flaws.

"The DEI accreditation standard, from the moment it was adopted, conflicted with controlling Supreme Court rulings and the plain text of the Civil Rights Act," Rubinstein said, urging the Trump administration to permanently strip the ABA of its federal status. "The ABA's leadership has made it clear, publicly and otherwise, that it will return to its unlawful ideological agenda at its first opportunity."

For more than 70 years, the ABA has operated as the sole federally recognized accreditor for U.S. law schools, granting the organization a near-monopoly over the legal profession. In almost every state, students must graduate from an ABA-accredited law school to be eligible to sit for the bar exam. Furthermore, the federal government uses the ABA's accreditation as the gatekeeper for Title IV federal student aid, meaning law schools must secure the group's stamp of approval for their students to receive federal loans.
BEAUTY SCHOOL MOMS CAUGHT IN ACCREDITATION CROSSFIRE AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION WEIGHS CONSEQUENTIAL DECISION

If Under Secretary Kent ultimately moves to strip the ABA of its recognition, the decision would effectively break that national monopoly. While law schools affiliated with larger universities could rely on their broader institutional accreditors to maintain access to federal financial aid, roughly a dozen stand-alone law schools would be forced to scramble for alternative accreditation. State supreme courts would also face immediate pressure to rewrite their bar admission rules to allow graduates from non-ABA schools to take the exam.
Students take the bar exam. (shu.edu)

Some states have already begun taking matters into their own hands to bypass the ABA's grip. Because the legal profession is regulated directly by the judicial branch, state supreme courts hold the ultimate authority to set educational requirements for bar admission.
TRUMP ADMIN URGES RETURNING EDUCATION TO STATES, CITING $3 TRILLION OF TAXES SPENT AND POOR PROFICIENCY SCORES

In January, Texas became the first state in the nation to eliminate its reliance on the ABA for law school accreditation, with the Texas Supreme Court finalizing a rule to take over the approval process itself. Just nine days later, the Florida Supreme Court followed suit.

By cutting ties with the organization, the Texas high court announced it would judge law schools on "simple, objective, and ideologically neutral criteria" rather than the ABA's mandates deemed by many as politically-driven.

Florida Solicitor General David Dewhirst speaks at a Federalist Society event in Washington, D.C., on the American Bar Association's "monopoly" over law school accreditation. Florida recently became among the first states in the country to strip the ABA of its exclusive accreditation power over future lawyers in its state. (Fox News Digital)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Other states are now catching on to the rebellion against the ABA. The Ohio Supreme Court formally proposed amendments in May to establish a state-run accreditation process, while supreme courts in Tennessee, Alabama and Washington have all recently taken steps to bypass the organization's monopoly.

"The ABA’s cartel-like control over law school accreditation drives up costs, limits access, and pushes ridiculous ideological mandates over merit," Trump's DOJ said earlier this year. "Ending the Tennessee Supreme Court’s exclusive reliance will expand opportunity AND lower costs."
Rubinstein noted that transferring authority back to the states marks a long-overdue correction for legal education.

"State supreme courts are ultimately responsible for certifying and disciplining attorneys—there is arguably no need for a middleman," Rubinstein told Fox News Digital. "By returning actual authority over legal education directly to the courts themselves... the result should be a better-quality education for attorneys and more accountability and transparency for the public."
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: AOC's Ivy League warmup act leads democratic socialists in notorious anti-Israel chant
summary: Cornell University's Young Democratic Socialists of America lead "from the river to the sea" chant before Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez takes stage.
story: Cornell University Young Democratic Socialists of America co-chairs Mina Petrova and Zoe Reisman warmed up the crowd at a Sunday event with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez by leading a "from the river to the sea" chant.
An event for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., saw her far-left hosts at Cornell University lead a packed crowd in singing the anti-Israel slogan "from the river to the sea" on Sunday.

The Cornell University Young Democratic Socialists of America hosted the event for AOC, which her campaign labeled as a "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall. The group's president, Mina Petrova, and co-Chair Zoe Reisman led the crowd of roughly 2,000 people in chanting "from the river to the sea," after declaring, "long live the student intifada."

"Cornell is fundamentally a capitalist institution that prioritizes billionaires and profit over students and community and is controlled by CEO trustees that are profiting off of genocide and war," Petrova told the crowd at one point, triggering applause.
BACKLASH ERUPTS OVER HASAN PIKER’S UPCOMING SPEAKING ENGAGEMENT AT CORNELL

The Democratic Socialists of America's Liberation Caucus is condemning Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., with a statement announcing the organization will not endorse her as a 2028 presidential candidate as speculation among potential candidates grows. (Getty Images)

"Here we stand as anti-imperialists and believe that nobody is disposable. We have a responsibility to stand in solidarity with oppressed peoples everywhere," Reisman said. "Student activism is not dead. Long live student resistance, and long live the student intifada."
YDSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.
30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS
AOC made no apologies when she eventually took the stage, joining her young hosts in accusing Cornell of censorship.

"Whether it’s the issue about Palestine or many others, whether it’s about people trying to fire those who are forming a union in their workplace, whether it’s people trying to speak up about a number of different issues, we have to respond to that first crackdown," she said.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Addresses A Crowd Of 36,000 People At The Fighting Oligarchy Rally At Gloria Molina Grand Park In Downtown Los Angeles On April 12, 2025. (Sam Ghazi/Middle East Images/Middle East Images via AFP)
AOC’S SOCIALIST CREDENTIALS FACE FRESH SCRUTINY AFTER GLARING 7-YEAR GAP SURFACES: ‘VERY CONVENIENT’
"When we come out in numbers, they cannot take us all," she added.
AOC's campaign says it is aimed at boosting voter turnout in Democrat strongholds, but recent polling shows that most Americans dislike association with Democratic Socialists of America groups.
HOUSE REPUBLICAN AIMS TO PUT DEMOCRATS ON THE RECORD OVER DSA WITH RESOLUTION CONDEMNING SOCIALISM
According to a recent Fox News Poll, 55% of registered voters hold an unfavorable view of the DSA, while only three in 10 see the DSA in a positive light.

An anti-Israel sign with the phrase "from the river to the sea Palestine will be free" at a protest near Tulane University in New Orleans. Jewish organizations have called the slogan antisemitic. (Credit: Ryan Zamos)

The Fox News Poll is the latest national survey to show that while the DSA has gained traction among Democrats, the group and the broader socialist movement in America face significant national skepticism.

The figures appear to reinforce a key element in the GOP midterm playbook, which aims to turn what's normally a referendum on the party in power into a choice election.
Fox News' Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

title: Woke megachurch pastor, Dem nominee called on congregation to repent for driving, eating beef
summary: Adam Hamilton, the Democrat seeking to be the first Kansans sent to the Senate in nearly a century, once asked his church congregation to repent for eating beef.
story: Adam Hamilton, the Democratic Senate nominee in Kansas — the nation's third-largest beef producer — told his congregation that cattle contribute to climate change. (Credit: YouTube/Church of the Resurrection, Jan. 27, 2020)
FIRST ON FOX: In Kansas, cows are king, but a Democrat trying to seize power once told his congregation to repent for eating beef and raising cattle.

Adam Hamilton, the Democratic nominee running to unseat Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in the Sunflower State, for years led the largest United Methodist church in the nation. He would give sermons that Marshall charged were "woke," and counter to Kansans' values.
One such sermon, reviewed by Fox News Digital, saw Hamilton call on his congregation to repent over their carbon footprints.
GOP SENATOR ALLEGES SCHUMER BEHIND 'HIT JOB' REPORT ON FORMER PATIENTS

Senior pastor Adam Hamilton spoke during "Heritage" services at 7:45 a.m. on Sunday, Sept. 16, 2012, in Wesley Covenant Chapel at the Church of the Resurrection in Leawood, Kansas. (Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

"That's what repentance means — I saw things differently, it changed my heart, and it changed my behavior," Hamilton said during a January 2020 sermon called, "What would Jesus say about climate change?"

"So what I'm calling you to today, and I'm calling myself to it, because I've been wasteful, I've done things that wasn't, you know, I didn't think about it, how it wasn't really good stewardship of the earth around me," he continued. "I'm calling us to repentance to say, ‘I realize that this has impact, even if it seems small, it has an impact on the world and future generations. And I feel badly about that, and I'm going to do something different from this time forward.’"

Despite Kansas’ 94-year history of being a ruby-red bastion for the GOP in the Senate, the race between Hamilton and Marshall has unexpectedly tightened in recent months as Republicans across the country face a sobering political environment.
BIG MONEY PROPELS DEM MEGACHURCH PASTOR TO VICTORY IN LONGSHOT KANSAS SENATE BID
Kansas slipped from "Likely R" in Fox News’ Power Rankings to "Lean R," and Cook Political Report echoed the same shift, too.

"In a state with more cattle than people, Hamilton saying that Kansans need repent for eating too much beef and flip flopping on the Farm Bill proves he’d be just like every other liberal Democrat in the Senate," Marshall told Fox News Digital in a statement.

High fuel prices, particularly diesel in an agriculture-centric state like Kansas, spurred by President Donald Trump’s Iran war are giving voters anxiety, and expanding the map of battleground states that Republicans need to defend to maintain their majority in the Senate.

Hamilton's campaign countered to Fox News Digital that Marshall has "repeatedly introduced legislation to reduce emissions from cattle and claimed 'everyone's concerned about the methane production in the cattle industry.'"

"Marshall even bragged how the decline of the herd 'eliminated half of the methane gas produced from cattle already,'" Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton, said. "As Adam said at the debate, Roger should repent for failing to stand up for Kansas cattle producers on tariffs, foreign imports, and skyrocketing diesel prices, and now he should repent for attacking Adam for something Roger Marshall said himself in the Senate. Kansas producers don't need lectures from someone who voted to put warning labels on hot dogs and bacon."

Meanwhile, Hamilton’s sermon was part scripture, part PowerPoint presentation on how greenhouse gases occur and their impact on the environment. And during his 44-minute talk, Hamilton suggested that one of Kansas’ staple economic drivers, beef, was a major contributor to the problem.
'WHY WOULD HE DO THIS TO US?': ONE CRUCIAL TRUMP DECISION IS HURTING HIS BASE, REPUBLICANS WARN
Cattle are herded at Lew Thompson's ranch on June 17, 2026, in Frio County, Texas. (San Antonio Express-News via Getty Images)

"Some of the things that we grow, because we like to eat them, like cattle, end up producing more carbon dioxide than other crops that we could grow, other forms of food that we could have," Hamilton said. "And so, in all of these ways, we are creating or adding to the amount of greenhouse gases in our world."

Cattle is a major industry for Kansas, which is the nation’s third-largest producer of beef, according to the Kansas Livestock Association. There are more heads of cattle in the state, just over 5.8 million, than people, with the state’s population sitting at roughly 2.9 million.
It provides a major cash influx for the state’s economy, too, with cattle farming and ranching producing tens of billions of dollars and employing over tens of thousands of Kansans.

"It is disappointing that a candidate for the U.S. Senate in Kansas, one of the nation’s top beef-producing states, would make a statement like this to his parishioners about beef’s impact on the climate," Kansas Livestock Association Chief Executive Officer Matt Teagarden told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Beef is an important, nutritious part of the American diet, and cattle play a significant role in maintaining grassland health and conservation, while accounting for only 2% of total U.S. greenhouse gas emissions."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Still, six years ago, Hamilton was calling on his congregation to change their habits to reduce their carbon footprint.

"Now, you got to do everything you can to reduce your own usage of fossil fuels, but maybe changing your diet so that the things that you eat are requiring less production that creates methane and carbon dioxide and everything else," Hamilton said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Sen Kennedy says no living politicians should have buildings named after them after Trump's moves
summary: Sen. John Kennedy has proposed barring living politicians from having buildings named after them as Trump pushes to rename the Kennedy Center.
story: Workers begin removing Donald Trump's name from the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C. following a federal appeals court ruling. The court denied a last-minute appeal to keep Trump's name on the building, which had been added after a unanimous board vote in December.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Sunday that living public officials should not have buildings named after them and proposed a rule to prohibit such renaming efforts.

This comes as President Donald Trump continues to push to rename the Kennedy Center after himself. The president has also sought to rename other prominent federal buildings in Washington, D.C., after himself since returning to the White House last year.
Kennedy said public officials, including Trump, should not "spend public money on private ads for themselves."
"The White House sees it differently, but … you can’t spend public money to … promote yourself," Kennedy told host Margaret Brennan during an appearance on CBS News' "Face the Nation."
KENNEDY CENTER CEILING PARTIALLY COLLAPSES AS TRUMP-LED BOARD PUSHES FOR 2-YEAR CLOSURE
Sen. John Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, speaks during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Kennedy's comments came as a new ad promoting Trump appeared on multiple networks that was funded by the federal government.
The senator then suggested public officials should be barred from having a building named after them while they are still alive.

"I may end up with a sombrero on my head, but I also think we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him when he’s alive," he said, referring to Trump mocking Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., last year by sharing AI videos of the lawmakers wearing sombreros.
FEDERAL JUDGE ORDERS TRUMP'S NAME REMOVED FROM KENNEDY CENTER, SAYS ONLY CONGRESS CAN RENAME IT

People watch construction workers build scaffolding near the Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts sign in Washington, D.C., on June 12, 2026. The Kennedy Center board sought an emergency appeal to block a court order requiring the removal of President Trump's name, but a judge denied the request. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Trump has attempted to rename multiple buildings after himself since returning to the Oval Office, including the Kennedy Center, although federal judges blocked multiple attempts by the center's board — handpicked by Trump — to add the president’s name to the building.
Trump's name was briefly added to the building's facade but was ordered removed after courts ruled that only Congress holds the authority to change the center's name.

The State Department also added Trump’s name last year to the U.S. Institute of Peace, but former institute officials removed by the Trump administration filed a court motion earlier this month to block construction crews from putting the president’s name onto the outside of the building.
Workers affix signage adding President Donald Trump's name on the facade of the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C. on Friday, Dec. 19, 2025. (Al Drago/Getty Images)
Trump also suggested he wanted New York's Penn Station and the D.C.-area's Dulles Airport named after him as a condition for a funding deal earlier this year.
The president has additionally floated a project to construct a promenade connecting the back of the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River, saying that allies wanted to call it the "Trump Promenade."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"They want to call it the Trump Promenade, but I don't know if I want to do that, but it's going to be beautiful," he said at the time.

title: Susie Wiles reveals brutal toll of fighting cancer while running Trump’s White House
summary: Susie Wiles reveals what it was like to undergo chemotherapy while leading the White House staff, saying some days just getting out of bed was a test.
story: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles says she is cancer-free after undergoing treatment. Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy reports on Wiles' announcement on 'America Reports.'

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is opening up about the grueling reality of fighting breast cancer while holding one of Washington's most demanding jobs, revealing that some days simply getting out of bed and going to work took all the strength she had.
In an op-ed published Sunday in USA Today, Wiles described what it was like to undergo chemotherapy while continuing to lead the White House staff for President Donald Trump.
The disease occupied her thoughts from the moment she woke up and sometimes even while she slept, she wrote.

"Fighting cancer is brutal and unrelenting," Wiles wrote. Questions about treatment, test results and what might come next could overtake even a strong mind. At times, she acknowledged, they overtook hers.
CANCER-RELATED BRAIN FOG MAY IMPROVE WITH 2 SIMPLE TREATMENTS, SCIENTISTS SAY

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles looks on during a roundtable to "save college sports" in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on March 6, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski / AFP via Getty Images)

Some days, Wiles said, she poured her strength into fighting the disease. On others, getting out of bed, getting dressed and going to work was its own test. "Most days, I carried the full weight of both," she wrote.

Work gave her a purpose beyond appointments, scans and side effects. "Cancer can make your world very small," Wiles wrote. She said she pushed herself to stay focused on the people who depended on her, even as she knew others might question whether she could still lead effectively.
KAI TRUMP REVEALS HOW FAMILY RALLIED AROUND MOM VANESSA AMID BREAST CANCER BATTLE: ‘IT’S A LONG JOURNEY’
Susie Wiles, White House chief of staff, during a roundtable in the Cabinet Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on Monday, Dec. 8, 2025. (Yuri Gripas/Abaca/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The treatment did take a toll on her stamina, mobility and, at times, her focus. Wiles said she could not always be everywhere she wanted to be. Colleagues inside and outside the White House stepped in, while her two daughters, extended family, friends and medical team helped carry her through the illness.
Wiles made clear that working through treatment would not be right or possible for everyone. For her, she wrote, the job helped her hold on to a sense of who she was beyond the disease.
CANCER SURVIVORS MAY SEE SURPRISING BENEFITS FROM ONE SPECIFIC EXERCISE, STUDY SAYS

U.S. President Donald Trump reacts as Director of the Presidential Personnel Office Sergio Gor and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles sit next to him on the day of a meeting with U.S. ambassadors at the White House in Washington, D.C., March 25, 2025. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)
After successful surgery, pathology showed no residual cancer, Wiles wrote. She said she now faces the work of rebuilding what treatment took from her.
"Chemotherapy is, in a word, a b----," she wrote.
DOLLY PARTON’S PRIVATE CANCER BATTLE HIGHLIGHTS WHY SOME PATIENTS DON’T SHARE THEIR DIAGNOSES
In a post on X Sunday, Wiles said she rarely writes about herself but wanted to share what it was like to fight cancer while continuing to do a job she loves.
"Cancer tried to make my world smaller. I was determined not to let it," she wrote, adding that she hoped her account could offer strength to someone still fighting the disease.
VANESSA TRUMP REVEALS BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS IN EMOTIONAL STATEMENT: 'I AM STAYING FOCUSED AND HOPEFUL'

President Donald Trump, right, with his chief of staff Susie Wiles as they meet with ambassador nominees in the Cabinet Room at the White House in Washington, DC on March 25, 2025. (John McDonnell/For The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Wiles announced Sept. 16 that she was cancer free after receiving clear pathology results following an appointment at the Mayo Clinic. She had disclosed her early-stage breast cancer diagnosis in March.

Trump praised Wiles during her treatment, saying in a prerecorded May tribute that she was winning her cancer battle. Wiles thanked him for his kindness and compassion, and credited her family, friends, colleagues and doctors with helping her through the ordeal.

For others going through treatment, Wiles offered a message of hope. "Cancer does not have to take away who you are," she wrote. She said that for her, life beyond the disease includes serving Trump and the country and being a mother, grandmother and friend.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

One of those daughters, Katie Wiles, responded to her mother’s account on X. "A strong woman isn’t loud in her strength; she’s steady and unshakable," she wrote. "You are our champion. So incredibly proud of you, Mom."
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: John Fetterman accidentally calls himself a 'lifelong Republican' at Texas Tribune Festival
summary: John Fetterman accidentally called himself a "lifelong Republican" at the Texas Tribune Festival, sparking laughs before clarifying his Democratic ties.
story: Sen. John Fetterman, D-PA, triggered a wave of laughs at a speaking event on Saturday, Sept. 26, after mistakenly referring to himself as a "life-long Republican." (Texas Tribune via Facebook)
Sen. John Fetterman, D-PA, triggered a wave of laughs at a speaking event on Saturday after mistakenly referring to himself as a "lifelong Republican."
Fetterman made the statement while on stage at the Texas Tribune Festival, going on to quickly correct himself and assert that he has no reason to abandon the Democratic Party.
The moment came when an attendee at the event asked why Fetterman doesn't run as an independent.
MAVERICK DEMOCRAT SURGES WITH REPUBLICANS AS HIS OWN PARTY TURNS ON HIM, STOKING TALK OF GOP SWITCH
Sen. John Fetterman, D-PA, triggered a wave of laughs at a speaking event on Saturday after mistakenly referring to himself as a "lifelong Republican." (Joseph A. Wulfsohn/Fox News Digital.)
"Because I’m a lifelong Republican," he said, realizing his mistake. "I guarantee you that will break through. That will get clipped."
Fetterman gave a keynote address earlier in the event where he elaborated on his criticisms of both the Republican and Democratic parties.
FETTERMAN WINS PRAISE FOR 'GUTS' AFTER GOING TOE-TO-TOE WITH JON STEWART OVER ISRAEL SUPPORT

"I don’t have a reason to," Fetterman said of joining Republicans. "But for a big-tent situation, it’s easier to be included in that big tent to say America deserved 9/11 or America is worse than Al-Qaida than being very proud to stand on the side of Israel."
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., leaves the Senate floor at the U.S. Capitol on July 15, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
Fetterman admitted he believed he has "no path as a Republican," but acknowledged that many Democrats are frustrated by his willingness to work with the opposing party.
FETTERMAN FACES DEM REVOLT AS BOMBSHELL REPORT FUELS PUSH TO OUST HIM: 'DISGRACE'
"If the Democratic Party votes me out or expels me, they’re always entitled to do that," he said.

Fetterman has been welcomed with open arms by Republicans to join the party after he floated leaving his own caucus and spurred further speculation that he would jump ship after dropping a video introducing his colleague, Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention earlier this month.
FETTERMAN TEASES WHERE HIS TRUE LOYALTY LIES AFTER SURPRISE APPEARANCE AT GOP CONVENTION

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gifts Democratic Sen. John Fetterman a silver-plated pager, commemorating the operation that used pagers against Hamas leaders and operatives. Fetterman visited Israel to show his support in its fight against the terrorist group that attacked on Oct. 7, 2023, killing more than 1,200 and taking many hostages. (GPO)
But the progressive-turned-centrist has repeatedly affirmed his Democratic ties, even as the knives have come out to cut him loose from the Senate.

Fetterman started his career in the Senate after besting Dr. Mehmet Oz in a tight race for power in 2022, where he clinched a historically thin Democratic majority in 2022 running on a progressive platform.
But since then, he has become a thorn in Democrats’ side and challenged the direction of the party.

Earlier this year, Fetterman warned that if Democrats became more entrenched in anti-Israel policy positions, he would exit the party, and has taken jabs at the party’s direction during this midterm election cycle as far-left progressives, like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, have emerged as standard-bearers.
Fox News Digital's Alex Miller contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Texas voters have plenty to say about whether Lone Star State could turn blue
summary: Texas voters at the State Fair of Texas reveal how inflation and economic frustration are shaping the Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton races this fall.
story: Fox News Digital asked voters at the Texas State Fair whether the reliably Republican state could become more competitive as the midterm elections approach.
DALLAS — Everything is bigger in Texas, including the political stakes this November.

Texas voters head to the polls Nov. 3 in an election that could reshape the state's political landscape, with major battles for governor, U.S. Senate and seats in Congress and the state legislature. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott faces Democrat Gina Hinojosa, while Republican Ken Paxton squares off against Democrat James Talarico for a U.S. Senate seat.

At the State Fair of Texas in Dallas, voters told Fox News Digital that pocketbook pressures are shaping how they view the state's future, with some predicting the reliably red Lone Star State will stay that way while others see an opening for Democrats this fall.
REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE

Briana photo caption Briana, a voter from Garland, Texas, told Fox News Digital at the State Fair of Texas that she expects the Lone Star State to remain red, despite a potentially tougher political fight. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)
"I think we're going to struggle, but I think it will stay red," Briana of Garland, told Fox News Digital.
Mike and Tracey, a couple from Houston, were more definitive.
"Red. It's going to stay red," Tracey said. "Red," Mike added.
Chris took that confidence a step further.
"Hell will freeze over before Texas flips blue," Chris told Fox News Digital.
Patrick and Jennifer, of Dallas, shared that confidence.
"Texas will always be a Republican state," Jennifer said, while acknowledging that Republican candidates will not win every race. "But we still think it will stay Republican," Patrick added.
Not everyone at the fair was betting on Texas staying firmly in Republican hands.
WE ASKED AMERICANS TO GRADE THE ECONOMY. THEN WE ASKED IF IT WOULD CHANGE THEIR VOTE.
Patrick and Jennifer, voters from Dallas, told Fox News Digital at the State Fair of Texas that they expect the Lone Star State to remain Republican. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)
Mary said she believes the Dallas-Fort Worth area is moving in the opposite direction.
"It's definitely leaning more blue. Texas as a whole, I'm not sure," she said. "I think if there would be an election that swings blue, it would be this one. So we'll see if it happens."
Party politics aside, several voters said the economy remains top of mind.

Cynthia, who moved to Texas from New York, said she is looking for policies that will grow the economy, support businesses and leave families with enough disposable income to enjoy outings like the State Fair.
FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS
Mike and Cynthia, voters from Houston, told Fox News Digital at the State Fair of Texas that they expect the Lone Star State to remain firmly red. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)
"If you don't have enough disposable income, then you can't really enjoy something like this," she said. "It's pricey."
Jennifer also pointed to inflation and the prolonged strain of higher prices.
"I think people were expecting some sort of inflation," Jennifer said. "But I don't think we were prepared for it to last this long."
Meanwhile, Roxanne also expressed frustration with the country's current direction, saying dissatisfaction with the current administration is influencing her political outlook.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Voters at the State Fair of Texas in Dallas spoke with Fox News Digital about the issues on their minds and the Lone Star State's political future ahead of the November elections. (Chris Torres/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service/Getty Images)
"I just don't agree with the current administration, so I really want to see somebody else come in and do a better job," she said.

From the midway to the ballot box, Texas voters offered competing views of where the Lone Star State is headed, but agreed the economy will be difficult to ignore as they prepare to cast their ballots Nov. 3.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Irish PM rejects antisemitism concerns in Ireland amid dramatic vote over boycotting Israel game
summary: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin rejected antisemitism claims as Ireland's soccer players held a dramatic last-minute vote on playing against Israel.
story: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin explains Irelands stance on Israel, the conflict in Gaza and concerns over antisemitism, while explaining how Irelands own history shapes its approach.

NEW YORK – Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin rejected claims that Ireland's sharp criticism of Israel has crossed into antisemitism as tensions flared around a politically charged soccer match between the countries Sunday, with Irish players holding a last-minute vote over whether to boycott the game.

Martin, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital this week in New York, outlined why Ireland has taken such a staunch position against the Israeli government's conduct of the war in Gaza, calling its military response "absolutely disproportionate" while pressing Israel to "change strategy" and calling for increased humanitarian aid to Gaza.

Martin argued that Ireland's own history — particularly its experience ending decades of conflict in Northern Ireland — gives the country a role to play as a voice for peace on the international stage, a theme he returned to while discussing Ukraine and the ongoing debate over Irish reunification.
"I think for the vast majority of people it does not," Martin said when asked directly whether anti-Israel sentiment in Ireland had crossed the line into antisemitism.
"We have no toleration for antisemitism, none," Martin added.
NEW YORK TIMES ISSUES CORRECTION, DELETES LINE QUESTIONING IF ISRAELIS WERE VICTIMS OF OCT 7 TERROR ATTACK

Celtic supporters display a "Stop The Game" banner during a match against Hearts at Celtic Park in Glasgow, Scotland, on May 16, 2026, as part of a campaign opposing Ireland's upcoming soccer fixtures against Israel. (Ross Parker/SNS Group via Getty Images; John Lamparski/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The extraordinary player vote came after months of pressure surrounding the UEFA Nations League fixture on Sunday, with more than 160 Irish sports figures calling for a boycott and players themselves publicly questioning whether the match should go ahead.
A "significant majority" of players ultimately voted on Saturday to play the game, while one player left the squad after expressing his wish not to take part.
In the interview, Martin strongly condemned Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack and defended Israel's right to exist in security.
"First of all, we condemned, absolutely, the outrageous terrorist attack by Hamas in October," Martin told Fox News Digital.

"We believe in a two-state solution," Martin said. "We believe that Israel, of course, has a right to exist in security and its people need to be guaranteed of security. But likewise, Palestinians should have a right to live in their homeland in a peaceful way."
"There are many peaceful voices in Palestine that I've met who want peaceful coexistence with Israel."
Martin said Ireland's strongly pro-Palestinian position was rooted partly in its own history.

"There's a very strong pro-Palestinian position in Ireland," Martin said. "Ireland, the Irish government and the Irish people, probably because of our own history, but also because of a sense of right and justice and fairness."
Supporters protest during the international friendly soccer match between the Republic of Ireland and Qatar at Aviva Stadium in Dublin on May 28, 2026. (Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile)
Thousands have taken to the streets across Ireland since the war began, while national broadcaster RTÉ refused to air this year's Eurovision Song Contest after Israel's participation was confirmed.
Ireland spent centuries under British rule before most of the island gained independence a little more than a century ago, while Northern Ireland remains part of the United Kingdom.
He said Israel's military response to the Oct. 7 attack had resonated deeply in Ireland and called for increased humanitarian aid into Gaza.

"We want humanitarian aid going into Gaza. There's not enough humanitarian aid going in," Martin said, pointing to the conditions facing roughly 2 million people there, including shortages of food and shelter and children without access to education.
Martin said Ireland wanted Israel to reconsider its conduct of the war, asking whether it would "change strategy" and "change its approach to the whole issue."
"So that's the background to the Irish position," he said. "People are angry in terms of what's going on in the Middle East and that's the manifestation of it."

Dublin , Ireland - 6 September 2025; Republic of Ireland supporters make their feelings know as they protest against Israel before the FIFA World Cup 2026 Group F qualifying match between Republic of Ireland and Hungary at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin. (David Fitzgerald/Sportsfile via Getty Images)
ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson said his players were uncomfortable with the games, declaring: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide." The Israeli Football Association accused him of "stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy," prompting Martin to call the remarks "unacceptable."

The FAI previously sought Israel's suspension from international competition. Separately, Irish soccer officials later voted to fulfill the Israel fixtures after being warned a boycott could cost the association at least $6.3 million and trigger UEFA sanctions.
Sunday's game will be played in Hungary, while Ireland's Oct. 4 home fixture has been moved to Serbia and will be played behind closed doors. Irish supporters will not have access to either game.

An organized campaign dubbed #StopTheGame has, meanwhile, spent months pressuring Irish soccer officials and players not to fulfill the Israel fixtures, staging protests and urging the national team to refuse to play.

The campaign has also spilled onto the field. During a friendly against Qatar in May, protesters threw tennis balls bearing "Stop The Game" messages onto the pitch in opposition to the Israel fixtures.
Martin has resisted calls for Ireland to boycott Israel, arguing that unilateral action could be "self-defeating" and may hurt Irish soccer without having any effect on Israel.

Republic of Ireland's Evan Ferguson looks on as play is halted after protesters threw tennis balls onto the pitch during an international friendly against Qatar at Aviva Stadium in Dublin on May 28, 2026. The protest targeted Ireland's upcoming soccer fixtures against Israel. (Charles McQuillan/Getty Images)
The dispute over the games reflects a broader debate over whether Ireland's criticism of Israel has crossed a line.

The American Jewish Committee raised concerns directly with Martin in Washington in March 2025 about antisemitism and what it called the "vilification of Israel in Ireland." An Anti-Defamation League official also participated in the meeting. The AJC alleged that antisemitism had become "pervasive" in Ireland.

Martin pointed to Ireland's annual Holocaust commemorations and the historic contribution of Jewish communities in Dublin, Cork and elsewhere in rejecting the suggestion that antisemitism was broadly tolerated in Ireland. He also pointed to Ireland's participation in international efforts against antisemitism and said the country campaigns against it globally.
"We cherish that contribution that the Jewish community has made to Ireland," Martin said.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 24, 2026. Martin used his address to criticize Israel's conduct in Gaza and Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank. (Angela Weiss/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Martin's defense of Ireland's position came before he addressed world leaders at the United Nations on Thursday, where he delivered a sharply critical assessment of Israel's conduct in Gaza and the West Bank, declaring that the international community had "failed Palestine."

"When the full truth of what has happened, what is still happening in Gaza, is finally known, when the evidence is gathered, when the testimonies are heard, when the true horrors are finally and fully revealed, it will shame the world," he said. "Nobody will be able to say that we did not know."
Martin accused violent Israeli settlers in the West Bank of acting with "near-total impunity" and said Palestinian communities faced displacement and destruction "amounting to ethnic cleansing."
He reiterated his support for a two-state solution, saying the only viable outcome was for "a State of Palestine and a State of Israel" to live side by side "in peace, security and dignity."

During his Fox News Digital interview, Martin connected Ireland's position on the Middle East to its experience ending decades of violence in Northern Ireland, saying "we feel we can make a contribution to that conflict resolution pathway."

That role has taken on added significance as Ireland holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union, giving it an elevated diplomatic role at a time of multiple international conflicts.

Martin also pointed to a personal experience that shaped his thinking, recalling meeting Israeli Rami Elhanan and Palestinian Bassam Aramin in Israel, two fathers who each lost a daughter in the conflict and later worked together for peace. Their stories are told in Colum McCann's novel "Apeirogon."
"That's an inspiration to me," Martin said, adding that he had met both men in Israel. He said their work reflected Ireland's own efforts to reconcile communities divided by generations of conflict.
Palestinians seek aid supplies from the U.S.-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), in the central Gaza Strip, Aug. 4, 2025. (REUTERS/Stringer)

Beyond the Middle East, Martin addressed Russia's war in Ukraine, saying a ceasefire along existing battle lines could provide a starting point for negotiations while rejecting territorial gains by force.

"Ukraine can't cede territory that Russia hasn't even conquered, despite four years of war," Martin said. "From our perspective, no one has the right to go into another country and take its territory."

Ireland has maintained its military neutrality while providing humanitarian and non-lethal assistance to Ukraine and taking in more than 120,000 Ukrainians since Russia's invasion. Martin rejected suggestions that such support compromised Ireland's neutrality, noting that Dublin has not supplied lethal weapons. "We want the war to end," he said.

Martin's focus on ending long-running conflicts also extends to Ireland's own divided island. He and his Fianna Fáil party support reunification with Northern Ireland, but he said greater trust between the two communities must come first.
"I believe in unity and my party believes in unity, but we have to work on it," Martin said. "We have to build reconciliation amongst the different traditions on the island of Ireland."

Under the Good Friday Agreement, a referendum would be called if it appeared likely that a majority in Northern Ireland supported reunification — an issue that gained fresh attention when Trump said during his recent visit to the country that he would "love" to see a united Ireland.
Martin also pointed to Ireland's unique relationship with the United States, crediting Washington with playing a "critical" role in the Northern Ireland peace process in the 1990s.
Asked whether Washington could play a role again in a future reunification process, he replied: "To a degree maybe, potentially, yeah."
Michael Dorgan is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business.

title: Trump's Greenland obsession isn’t random. Here’s what’s at stake
summary: Greenland's untapped rare earth minerals, oil and gas reserves could reshape U.S. energy security as Trump's Denmark deal expands military presence.
story: Robert Price, CEO of Greenland Energy Company and president of USFM Corporation, says the agreement could bolster long-term investment and US security as China, Russia loom over critical mineral supplies.
Greenland may be covered in ice, but beneath its surface could be resources critical to the global economy — including rare earth minerals, nickel, copper, palladium, cobalt, oil and natural gas.
The Arctic island’s location is just as valuable.

Positioned between North America and Europe, Greenland sits along key military and shipping routes. As conflicts in Ukraine and Iran expose vulnerabilities in global energy and supply chains, the island has become increasingly important to the United States and other world powers.
WHY TRUMP ZEROED IN ON GREENLAND, THE WORLD’S LARGEST ISLAND, MOSTLY COVERED IN ICE — IN 3 CHARTS

A composite image shows President Donald Trump overlaid on a protest in Greenland. Trump announced an agreement concerning U.S. security interests in Greenland, while Denmark and Greenland have emphasized that the deal preserves their sovereignty and territorial integrity. (Sean Gallup/Getty Images; rtur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Those factors help explain why President Donald Trump has spent years pushing for greater American control and influence in Greenland and why his administration recently reached a new security agreement with Denmark and Greenland.
The deal, which Trump signed on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, will expand the U.S. military presence on the island while keeping Greenland under Danish sovereignty.
Here are three reasons Greenland has become one of the world’s most strategically important places.
The United States is seeking to reduce its dependence on China and Russia for critical minerals used in electronics, batteries, energy infrastructure and defense technology.

"We don’t want to be dependent on China for our rare earth minerals, and we don’t want to be dependent on Russia for them either," Robert Price, CEO of Greenland Energy Company and president of USFM Corporation, told Fox News Digital.
FLOURISH CHART EMBED HERE: 30309299

Price’s USFM is exploring nickel, copper, palladium and cobalt deposits around Disko Island in western Greenland. He said the region could eventually rival Russia’s mineral-rich Norilsk district, though its potential remains unproven as drilling continues.
Greenland’s melting ice is opening new Arctic shipping routes and exposing critical mineral resources, adding to the island’s growing strategic importance. (Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/Getty Images)

Greenland’s potential riches extend beyond minerals. Price’s Greenland Energy Company is pursuing permits for an exploratory oil well planned for 2027 on the island’s eastern side, where he said the geology resembles the petroleum-producing North Sea.
"Our licenses are similar to the same petroleum system as the North Sea," Price said, adding that the company has sampled oil on and below the surface.
TRUMP'S AMBITIOUS ENERGY BET COULD BE A WINNING HAND AS THE WORLD BURNS MORE OIL, GAS THAN EVER
The project comes as the Iran war disrupts global energy markets and threatens shipping through the Strait of Hormuz a critical artery for the world’s oil supply.
"One of the reasons that we are exploring for oil in Greenland is because of what’s going on in the Strait of Hormuz right now," Price said.
Greenland’s oil and gas potential remains unproven and would require additional permits, exploration and investment.

Pituffik Space Base in Greenland serves as the U.S. military’s northernmost installation and supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance. (Thomas Traasdahl/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images)
Greenland’s strategic value also comes from its location between North America and Europe, near key air, sea and missile routes connecting the United States, Russia and Europe.

The U.S. has maintained a military presence on the island for decades. Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, is the northernmost Defense Department installation and supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance.
Melting Arctic ice is opening new shipping routes and increasing interest from the United States, Russia and China.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump’s agreement with Denmark and Greenland would expand the U.S. military presence while preserving Danish sovereignty, according to the administration. Price said the deal could also boost investor confidence in long-term oil, gas and mineral projects.
"What it does is it shores up long-term investment in Greenland, and that’s what our projects are," Price said. "They’re long-term investments from oil, gas and minerals."
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Trump reaffirms ICE arrest policy after confusing guidance sparks alarm among agents
summary: Trump told officials that anyone in the country illegally remains "on the table" for arrest and deportation after internal ICE guidance caused confusion.
story: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin discusses the priorities of President Donald Trump’s border agenda and the administration’s crackdown on illegal immigration on ‘The Will Cain Show.’
The Trump administration denied reports Saturday evening that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had temporarily instructed agents to limit arrests to illegal immigrants with criminal records.

The clarification comes as immigration enforcement remains a central pillar of President Donald Trump’s agenda. The administration has promised an aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration and expanded deportations, and officials said that effort has not been scaled back.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY

President Donald Trump has made immigration enforcement a central pillar of his administration, promising a sweeping crackdown on illegal immigration and expanded deportations. (David Peinado/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Fox News correspondent Bill Melugin, who spoke with Trump and nine ICE and Department of Homeland Security sources, reported that verbal guidance instructing field offices to prioritize the "worst first" was distributed nationwide earlier this week.
The guidance alarmed some ICE agents, who described it as shocking and frustrating, Melugin wrote on X.

Sources later said the confusion stemmed from internal conversations about prioritizing the most serious offenders and that the directive was the result of a "miscommunication," rather than a formal change in policy.
"There is no change in immigration enforcement policy," Melugin wrote on X.
New guidance was sent to ICE field offices Saturday evening to reaffirm that the administration’s enforcement policy had not changed, according to the sources.
DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents conduct enforcement operations nationwide as the Trump administration pledges to expand arrests and deportations of illegal immigrants. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg/Getty Images)
Trump told Fox News that ICE can still arrest and deport anyone who is in the country illegally.

ICE agents will also continue arresting illegal immigrants without additional criminal histories, including "collaterals," or individuals encountered during an operation targeting someone else.
The sources said the administration’s broader immigration enforcement agenda remains in place.

title: Iran ‘miscalculating’ by betting on midterms after 3-hour talks, Trump officials warn
summary: President Donald Trump says Iran is waiting on midterm elections to cut a deal, but Marco Rubio warns Tehran misreads U.S. presidential powers.
story: State Department Principal Deputy Spokesperson Tommy Pigott tells Fox News Digital the United States is pushing the United Nations to "get back to basics" as future funding remains tied to reforms.

NEW YORK — Trump officials say Iran is miscalculating if it believes rising prices and the midterm elections will weaken President Donald Trump's hand in negotiations to end the nearly seven-month conflict.
The administration is projecting confidence that mounting economic pressure will push Tehran toward a deal, even after three hours of talks this week ended without an announced breakthrough.
"The president holds all of the cards here," State Department principal deputy spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

Americans, meanwhile, are facing a mounting cost at home. The national average for regular gasoline reached $4.49 per gallon Friday, according to AAA, up from $3.16 a year ago. AAA said volatility in the Strait of Hormuz and high crude oil prices have driven the national average to its highest level ever recorded for this time of year.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged those costs Wednesday while arguing that allowing Iran to eventually obtain a nuclear weapon would carry a far greater price.
THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES
President Donald Trump delivers remarks to the United Nations General Assembly at the UN headquarters in New York City on Sept. 23, 2025. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
"It comes at a price and at a cost, there's no doubt about it," Rubio told reporters. "But the cost of not doing something about it is substantially higher, especially for future generations."

Trump himself laid out the stakes in stark terms during his address to the U.N. General Assembly Tuesday, presenting Tehran with a choice between reaching a deal that would allow Iran to rebuild or facing potentially devastating further U.S. action.

"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said. "Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"
But Trump predicted Tehran would ultimately choose a deal, arguing that Iranian leaders are waiting to see whether the November midterm elections weaken his position.
"They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," Trump said. "What they don't realize is that I'm not running."
"I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran," Trump added. "It doesn't even enter my mind."
A U.S. official told Fox News Digital Friday that discussions through mediators remained "positive and constructive," but said the administration was in no hurry to reach an agreement.

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush," the official said, adding that nearly 40 million barrels of oil had transited the strait over the previous 48 hours. The official predicted oil and gas prices would fall back to pre-conflict levels as the U.S. continues to maintain control of the strait.

Trump said U.S. officials held a "very good" three-hour meeting with Iranian officials Tuesday as part of a renewed diplomatic push to end the conflict. But Rubio cautioned Wednesday against characterizing the talks as a "major breakthrough," saying they were largely a continuation of previous conversations.
"I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation," Rubio said.

Rubio also said the administration would make public any "good outcomes or things to announce jointly" stemming from its diplomatic engagements. No such announcement immediately followed the Iran meeting.

Iran has since put forward a proposal of its own. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran presented U.S. mediators with a seven-day plan this week that would restore passage through the Strait of Hormuz at the end of the seven days if certain conditions are met, followed by renewed negotiations toward a broader agreement.
The proposal draws from the memorandum of understanding Trump and Iran reached in June. A mediator told CBS News the latest discussions were positive but remained in their early stages.

The stakes in Hormuz remain high. Commercial traffic through the critical oil chokepoint has been sharply disrupted during the conflict, although U.S. officials say the amount of oil moving through the strait is increasing.
TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN

"The diplomatic door is always open. The president is a deal maker," Pigott said. "But he's going to see the fundamental principle that they cannot have a nuclear weapon accomplished one way or another."
Pigott pointed to growing oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the economic pressure Washington has imposed on Tehran as evidence that the balance remains in Trump's favor.

"We are seeing oil move [through] the Strait of Hormuz, increasing every single day," Pigott said. "We're seeing the devastating effects on the Iranian regime from economic [actions]. Hundreds of millions of dollars are being denied to the regime through this blockade that we're seeing."
Rubio offered a similar assessment Wednesday when asked about Trump's assertion that Iran may be waiting for the outcome of the midterm elections before making a deal.

"I think the Iranians misread our system," Rubio said. "I think the Iranians are under this illusion that Democrats are going to win in November, and the president will no longer be able to do things against them."
Rubio said Congress remains an important branch of government but argued Tehran misunderstands the limits of congressional power over sanctions and military action.
"The president has extraordinary powers. Every president does," Rubio said. "He's the commander in chief, both constitutional and otherwise, to be able to carry out those functions."
"So I think that the Iranians are fundamentally misreading our political system," Rubio continued.

Soldiers from Iran's land, navy, air force and special forces parade during National Army Day on April 18, 2025, in Tehran, Iran. The country held its annual Army Day parade, which included an address by President Masoud Pezeshkian. (Getty Images)

The administration is also confronting threats to energy infrastructure elsewhere in the region. Iran-backed Houthi rebels have targeted Saudi Arabia as the conflict has expanded, adding another source of uncertainty for global energy markets.

Rubio said Wednesday that the restart of a Saudi pipeline following attacks was "critical for their economy" and "critical for the global economy." He said energy infrastructure had been targeted by the Houthis as well as Shiite militias in Iraq that the U.S. says are backed by Iran.
"Every time you guys ask me a question about the Middle East, it goes back to someone who's supported by Iran," Rubio said.
Rubio said the U.S. would continue honoring its defense commitments to Saudi Arabia while declining to discuss what additional military options Trump could consider.

"They are a strategic defense partner," Rubio said. "The U.S. made commitments to them. We will live up to those commitments. We are living up to those commitments now."

title: SCOTUS detention fight could unleash dangerous criminal migrants onto US streets, experts warns
summary: A Supreme Court battle over bond hearings for detained noncitizens with criminal records could make it harder for ICE to keep detainees locked up.
story: Chad Mizelle argues that allowing bond hearings after several months of detention would incentivize delay tactics and increase the risk that criminal migrants abscond.

A Supreme Court battle over whether certain noncitizens with criminal records are entitled to bond hearings during lengthy deportation proceedings could become a public safety concern by making it harder for the federal government to keep some detainees behind bars, legal experts warn.

The Trump administration is asking the justices to take up Genalo v. D.C., a case involving a Dominican citizen with four criminal convictions who has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement while fighting removal.

The dispute centers on a Second Circuit precedent requiring a bond hearing when mandatory immigration detention becomes "unreasonably prolonged." At that hearing, the government must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the detainee poses a flight risk or danger to the community.
MACHETE-WIELDING MS-13 GANGSTER WANTED FOR MURDER WALKS FREE AFTER BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE RELEASES HIM: DHS

Chad Mizelle, chair of litigation at the America First Policy Institute and a former acting associate attorney general and Justice Department chief of staff, told Fox News Digital the implications extend beyond immigration law.

"We are talking about criminal aliens here," Mizelle said. "Those are individuals who have been accused of or convicted of an aggravated felony. Accused or convicted of murder. Accused or convicted of child rape. Accused or convicted of grievous harm upon another human being."

Federal agents detain a man after attending a court hearing in immigration court at the Jacob K. Javitz Federal Building on June 30, 2025 in New York City. ((Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images))
"So these are the worst of the worst individuals," Mizelle continued. "Do we want those individuals walking the streets, re-committing, harming other individuals?"

Mizelle argued Congress imposed mandatory detention on certain noncitizens with criminal records to keep them detained during removal proceedings, while the Second Circuit’s prolonged-detention rule could incentivize some detainees to drag out their cases long enough to seek bond.
DOJ MOVES TO STRIP CITIZENSHIP FROM 17 PEOPLE ACCUSED OF HIDING DISTURBING CRIMES

The man at the center of the administration’s latest petition, identified in court papers as D.C., is a 62-year-old Dominican citizen who illegally entered the United States and has four criminal convictions, according to court records.

In 1997, D.C. was charged with multiple drug offenses, including selling and possessing a controlled substance. He failed to appear for trial, was convicted by a jury and sentenced in absentia to three to nine years in prison, but did not serve that sentence until 2024. In 2007, he was charged with possessing a forged instrument after presenting false identification to police and again failed to appear in court.

In 2016, D.C. faced several charges stemming from a domestic dispute, including second-degree strangulation, third-degree assault and acting in a manner to injure a child under 17. He pleaded guilty to criminal obstruction of breathing or blood circulation and also resolved his earlier forged-instrument case with a guilty plea. Later that year, he pleaded guilty to criminal contempt.

D.C. was finally arrested on the outstanding warrant from his 1998 drug conviction in April 2024. After completing his state sentence in September 2025, ICE immediately detained him while his removal proceedings continued.
FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT

WASHINGTON, DC - MARCH 17: The U.S. Supreme Court is shown March 17, 2025 in Washington, DC. The Trump administration defied a federal judge's court order this past weekend in a case related to the deportation of more than 200 alleged Tren de Aragua gang members to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act of 1789. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

The district court subsequently ordered that D.C. receive a bond hearing under binding Second Circuit precedent but denied his separate request for immediate release. The government is now asking the Supreme Court to take the case before the Second Circuit itself rules — an unusual procedure known as certiorari before judgment.
The administration turned to D.C.’s case after two other noncitizens at the center of the same legal fight saw their cases become moot.

One, Carol Williams Black, had been detained for roughly seven months. His case became moot after he received a final order of removal and permanently left the United States. Black was convicted of sexually abusing a child in 2000. The Supreme Court therefore granted review in June only as to the second detainee, G.M.

G.M., a lawful permanent resident from the Dominican Republic, pleaded guilty to second-degree assault in May 2015 after being accused of attacking and robbing a man during a 2012 incident in New York City. He was sentenced to two years in prison and was released early on parole in December 2016 after serving 19 months. ICE arrested G.M. at his home on Oct. 5, 2020, and detained him for 21 months without a bond hearing while removal proceedings continued.
TRUMP’S FIGHT OVER RARELY USED 18TH-CENTURY DEPORTATION LAW LIVES ON IN LATEST COURT CLASH

The Supreme Court was scheduled to hear his case Oct. 13. But in late August, New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul granted G.M. a full and unconditional pardon for the assault conviction that had formed the basis for his deportation proceedings and mandatory detention. Solicitor General John Sauer agreed the case was moot, and the Supreme Court dismissed it Sept. 11 without ruling on the merits.
The administration then identified D.C. as its replacement vehicle and asked the justices to hear the same constitutional questions this term.

Federal immigration officers consult as they wait for respondents to depart from their hearings to conduct targeted detainments at U.S. immigration court in Manhattan, in New York City, Oct. 24, 2025. (David 'Dee' Delgado/Reuters)
FEDERAL JUDGE TIES ICE AGENTS' HANDS WITH RULING ON WARRANTLESS SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ARRESTS
Carrie Severino, president of Judicial Crisis Network (JCN), said the dispute is likely to affect many similar immigration cases nationwide.

"This is not a question that's only going to affect D.C., the criminal Dominican national at issue in this case," Severino told Fox News Digital. "This is an issue that's going to affect criminal aliens across the country."
A victory by D.C. would impose new hurdles on the government, including additional hearings and use of resources, Severino said.

"As we know, immigration cases, skipping out on showing up for court dates is incredibly common," she added. "This is not something that I think the court ought to be granting on a regular basis that they'd be letting people out on bond simply on their word that they're going to be coming back when they know that they are likely to be removed."

Dozens of immigrants are detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents inside the Federal Plaza courthouse in New York City on Thursday, June 26, following their legal proceedings. The arrests, which took place shortly after court appearances, have sparked criticism from immigrant rights advocates, who say courthouse enforcement undermines due process and deters community members from seeking legal protection. (Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The case also raises questions about who must prove whether continued detention is necessary. The Second Circuit ruled that the government must prove by clear and convincing evidence that a detainee should remain in custody.

"And so, if the Supreme Court winds up affirming what the Second Circuit held, that means it's going to be harder for the government to be able to detain this particular population of criminal aliens or terrorism-linked aliens," Florida State University law professor Michael Morley told Fox News Digital. "There are going to be situations where the government is not able to show that a particular person is either likely to flee or poses a risk of danger and this dangerousness by a heightened or clear and convincing standard."

"It means that these criminal aliens who are already subject to removal proceedings are more likely to be released into the community while those underlying removal proceedings continue to make their way slowly through the adjudicative process," Morley continued.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Supreme Court has not yet agreed to hear D.C.’s case.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Michigan man doxxed after exposing his city's booming Islamic surge takes defiant stand: 'Not gonna stop'
summary: Justin Tye told Fox News Digital he won't back down after being doxxed for speaking out about mosques and Muslim immigrants in Warren, Michigan.
story: Several residents in the town of Warren, Michigan are expressing concerns that their town could become the next Dearborn as the Islamic population surges.
A Michigan man who is facing backlash for speaking out against the growing Islamic population in his town refused to back down during an interview with Fox News Digital.
"This is my home, this is where I was born and raised, this city, this state," said Justin Tye, 57, of Warren, Michigan.

Tye's address was doxxed in the wake of a Fox News Digital story where he described how his town and neighborhood have been transformed by mostly Muslim immigrants over the past decade or so. He said he's received some hate mail, including a package addressed to "Justin Tye, Bigot at Large."
Justin Tye stands on his front lawn in Warren, Michigan on Aug. 25, 2026. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)
WORKING-CLASS AMERICANS SAY THEIR TOWN IS THE NEXT DEARBORN — AND THEY'VE HAD ENOUGH
One package contained stickers reading "F— Trump and f— you for voting for him," along with a box of feminine hygiene products.
But Tye isn't afraid of any backlash.
"Some things are worth the trouble, and this is worth the trouble that could come from it," he said. "Being doxxed, I'm not afraid. I kind of figured this was gonna come with the territory."
He also vowed to keep speaking out.
BILL MAHER RIPS IMMIGRANTS WHO REFUSE TO ADAPT, SAYS AMERICAN VALUES ARE ‘NOT NEGOTIABLE’

"I'm not gonna stop. I mean, you come here from another country and you disrespect the people who have lived in this neighborhood for decades, and in many cases like myself, there's several people I went to school with that bought their parents' homes and live back here," he said, adding that he is speaking up for his neighbors too.

"And that's what I've been hearing mainly is, 'finally a voice,'" he said. "These people here, these Muslims ... you need to respect the people, the Americans that are here. Stop disrespecting the people that lived here for decades."
Tye said he's received encouragement from residents around town.

"I'm getting a lot of support," he said. Like I was out, I had to go do some shopping. I went to Meijer, I went to the bank, and then I stopped at a pizza place to get a pizza, and all three places I was stopped by people, asked if I was the Justin that was interviewed by Fox, and I said 'yes.' And the support I'm getting is incredible."
Tye and several of his neighbors spoke to Fox News Digital several weeks ago in Warren.
PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH'
"It all started when they bought the mosque, roughly six years ago," said Tye.

"After Ramadan, they would have their [Eid al-Fitr] prayer service. It was unannounced. We didn't know anything," he continued. "All of a sudden, we were just woken up to 100-plus people behind the mosque, with an imam on a podium with big amplifier speakers, belting out his prayer service. So it woke up the whole neighborhood."
TRUMP INAUGURATION PASTOR SAYS DEARBORN CHRISTIANS 'AFRAID' TO SPEAK OUT IN MUSLIM-MAJORITY CITY
He described his neighborhood now as "chaos."
He also took Fox News Digital on a guided tour of Warren, and pointed out five new mosques built or under construction within a seven-mile radius of his house.
SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT
An old industrial machinery business is now a mosque, as is a former Baptist church. Another towering mosque is under construction in the area.
"Seems like every restaurant that closes up — American restaurant — there's a Muslim restaurant that opens up. I've seen four or five of them so far," one of Tye's neighbors told Fox News Digital.
Justin Tye received a package addressed to "Bigot at Large" after exposing his city's booming Islamic population. (Justin Tye)
"I'm normally laid back. Things don't bother me," said another. "But it's like, this is my neighborhood and they're just taking it over, and that's what bothers me. And they don't care."
After the initial story was published, the city released a message on social media titled, "One Warren: Stronger Together, No Room for Hate."
Friday afternoon, the city responded to Tye's doxxing, and unequivocally denounced the practice.
"Every Warren resident deserves to feel safe in their own community. No one should have to fear being threatened, harassed, or intimidated, simply because they chose to speak up or raise a concern."
Jeff Tye points to a sign barring semi trucks from his neighborhood, as semi truck sits on the property of the Al-Ishaan Islamic Center behind it. (Peter D'Abrosca/ Fox News Digital)

"Targeting someone at their home crosses a line," the statement said. "A person’s home should be a place of safety and privacy, never a place where they are made to feel unsafe because of their views. Regardless of where we stand on an issue, every resident deserves dignity and respect."
The city noted that while not everyone will always see eye to eye, "disagreement should never become an excuse for personal attacks, intimidation, or retaliation."

"There is room for everyone in Warren. There is room for disagreement, debate, protest, and advocacy. But there is no room for threats, harassment, intimidation, or hate. We should hold ourselves and one another to a standard that protects both the safety of our neighbors and the freedom to speak openly."
